newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Merger talk highlights Lonrho value.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Merger talk highlights Lonrho value.

text.p: The value of Lonrho Plc, hidden behind a clutter of activities and subsidiaries, began to shine through on Monday following news it was in merger talks with South Africa's JCI Ltd.

Lonrho and JCI confirmed separately on Monday that they had held talks on a possible merger of the two groups. It would create one of the world's largest mining companies with a market capitalisation estimated at more than $3 billion.
"It (the negotiations) focuses attention on Lonrho being actually very cheap," said analyst Roger Chaplin at broker T. Hoare.
Lonrho shares rose six pence to 141 pence in late morning trade with several analysts estimating their asset value was around 50 pence higher.
The British conglomerate, whose activities range from mining to hotels to general trading, set out early last year to break up its sprawling empire.
But Lonrho had lost most of its lustre as plans to split itself up to reveal its treasures were slow to materialise.
Lonrho has so far only sold one of its two hotels chains and disposed of Lonrho Sugar earlier this month, but still has to demerge its African trading operations.

This would leave it with its extensive mining operations, which have now attracted the attention of JCI. Any merger with JCI might well coincide with the planned demerger of the South African trading businesses, analysts said.
But they said a JCI-Lonrho link-up was still far from a done deal, with other mining firms also interested in Lonrho's coal, platinum and gold activities.
It was likely that Lonrho would not only consider teaming-up with JCI, analysts said.
Market talk focused on South African firms such as Avmin Ltd and Randgold Resources as possible alternatives. But Australian firms might also be keen to strike a deal with Lonrho.
"Lonrho would be doing shareholders a disservice by not taking other offers into consideration," said Charles Kernot at Paribas Capital Markets.
A deal with JCI would make sense, adding a wealth of extra mining management expertise to Lonrho, he added.
A JCI-Lonrho link would also offer a way out for major stakeholder Anglo American in a deal which could prevent any major earnings dilution for Lonrho shareholders.
The European Union last month told Anglo to reduce its Lonrho stake to below 10 percent from its current 27.5 percent.
Kernot said Anglo could swap its stakes in both JCI and Lonrho for the latter's interest in Ashanti, the Ghanaian gold mining company.
He estimated that 41 percent in Ashanti could be worth 540 million pounds ($884.5 million), while Anglo's combined holdings in Lonrho and JCI would be worth around 450 million pounds.
"It would give the new entity complete independence...and Anglo would get Ashanti which is also something they would like," said Kernot.
